texts.29da0ab5aa4c: The trial aims to establish whether selective neck dissection in addition to resection of the primary tumour increases survival when compared with resection of the primary alone, among patients with early oral squamous cell carcinoma who have no clinical or radiological evidence of neck metastases. Additionally the trial aims to determine how SEND and complex reconstruction affect quality of life (QOL) and whether the use of SEND on all patients presenting with tumours measuring 1-3cms and clinically N0 necks represents a cost-effective use of resources.  We will also use the pathology results to try to identify risk factors for metastasis so that in the future elective neck dissection could be reserved for only those patients with an increased risk of neck metastasis based on their primary site pathological markers
texts.b4b83cfc6f9b: The trial aims to establish whether selective neck dissection in addition to resection of the primary tumour increases survival when compared with resection of the primary alone, among patients with early oral squamous cell carcinoma who have no clinical or radiological evidence of neck metastases. Additionally the trial aims to determine how SEND and complex reconstruction affect quality of life (QOL) and whether the use of SEND on all patients presenting with tumours measuring 1-3cms and clinically N0 necks represents a cost-effective use of resources. We will also use the pathology results to try to identify risk factors for metastasis so that in the future elective neck dissection could be reserved for only those patients with an increased risk of neck metastasis based on their primary site pathological markers. The incidence of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) in the UK is 4,400 new cases per year. It is the 6th commonest cancer worldwide and its incidence is rising. The cervical lymph nodes are the first point of metastatic spread for OSCC, and a significant cause of death. Unfortunately, pathology studies have shown that these neck metastases are not detectable clinically or radiologically in up to 35% of patients with early primary site disease. This has created controversy over the management of these patients. Some believe that an aggressive approach with elective removal of neck lymph nodes (END) improves disease control and survival, so the use of END is increasing both in the UK and abroad. However, others believe that survival is not improved with END. The overall question is, are we under-treating patients with occult neck metastases if we delay a neck dissection until they have clinically detectable neck disease, or are we over-treating patients who do not have occult neck disease if we perform an END at presentation? The proposed trial aims to resolve this issue. The trial is a multicentre randomised clinical trial which will be based on patients with early oral cancer (1-3 cm) who have no clinical or radiological evidence of neck metastasis. 652 patients will be randomised to receive either resection of the primary tumour alone or resection with simultaneous selective neck dissection. Patient recruitment is expected to take 4 years followed by 4 years follow-up. The main outcome is overall survival, which is why it is vital that we are able to ascertain if any patients who were enrolled in the study have died. Other outcomes are disease-free survival, recurrence, cost-effectiveness and quality of life. The primary objective of the trial is to determine whether SEND is associated with an increased survival compared to patients who are not offered this procedure. Forty surgeons from 30 UK centres have agreed to participate. This is a trial comparing two surgical procedures so blinding is not possible. The 2 trail interventions are: 1. Resection of primary tumour with simultaneous selective neck dissection at presentation, with or without reconstruction. 2. Resection of primary tumour alone and salvage treatment of the neck if neck metastases develop later.

texts.ee70d40fa2cb:
The role of selective neck dissection used electively in patients with early oral squamous cell carcinoma (1−3cm primary size) and no clinical evidence of lymph node metastases in the neck (N0)

The trial aims to establish whether selective neck dissection in addition to resection of the primary tumour increases survival when compared with resection of the primary alone, among patients with early oral squamous cell carcinoma who have no clinical or radiological evidence of neck metastases. Additionally the trial aims to determine how SEND and complex reconstruction affect quality of life (QOL) and whether the use of SEND on all patients presenting with tumors measuring 1-3cms and clinically N0 necks represents a cost-effective use of resources. 

We will also use the pathology results to try to identify risk factors for metastasis so that in the future elective neck dissection could be reserved for only those patients with an increased risk of neck metastasis based on their primary site pathological markers.

Data access is restricted to those named in section 7 of this agreement. Any changes will be notified to the NHS IC.
